Pele Yoetz 298:2: And the halachic authorities wrote that although according to the secret meaning of the matter it is impossible to say that one is entirely exempt from reading the Scripture twice and the Targum once, according to the plain meaning of the matter, the reading of the Targum was to understand the content, since in their time they spoke Aramaic. Behold, therefore, for us the essential commandment is to read every portion with Rashi's commentary, and for those who speak a foreign vernacular, in that vernacular. Behold, therefore, let the righteous man hold to his way, holding to this while also not letting go of that (Ecclesiastes 7:18), and there is a time for every purpose on the holy Sabbath day for one who does not waste the hours in idle sitting and idle talk. And there are already places where groups of people study, aggadic passage by aggadic passage, on the holy Sabbath — some study Psalms and some study Scripture, Mishnayot, Midrashim, and the like — happy are the Israelites, and happy are those of perfect way who walk in the good path.
Pele Yoetz 299:1: Pedut (Redemption) — The Holy One, blessed be He, has shown us great redemption, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Pesachim 111a): “Give thanks to the Lord, for He is good” — for He collects a person's debt through his own good fortune: the rich man through his ox, the poor man through his lamb, the widow through her hen. And they said in Midrash Kohelet (7:27), Rabbi Yitzchak said: a person stumbles into transgression and is liable for death at the hand of Heaven — with what is he atoned? His ox dies, his hen is lost, his flask breaks, he stubs his little finger and a drop of blood comes out — a part of the soul is like the whole soul. And so it is with every kind of pain and loss that comes upon a person, whether at the hand of man or at the hand of Heaven — it is all for his own good and for the redemption of his soul.
Pele Yoetz 299:2: And there was already an incident with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who was walking with Elijah the Prophet, of blessed memory, and they entered the house of a certain poor man who received them cheerfully and honored them greatly. And it happened at midnight that Elijah the Prophet arose and killed the man's cow, which was as dear to him as the apple of his eye, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi wondered greatly at this deed, until Elijah, of blessed memory, revealed his secret: that this was the fruit of his righteousness and the honor he had shown, for it had been decreed that his wife, dear to him as his own soul, should die, and his cow atoned for him instead (Otzar HaMidrashim, p. 211). And he further related a story of a man who spent much money so that his son would learn the science of astrology. And it came to pass on the day the son learned this wisdom that he went out to his father to be a stargazer, and his father said to him, “Tell me what you see concerning me.” He said to him, “I have seen that your horse will die.” What did he do? He went and sold it immediately. Again he gazed at the stars and told him that it was decreed upon his houses that they would burn; he went and sold them immediately. And so it continued in this manner, until finally he told him that it was decreed upon him that he would die. He began to cry out bitterly, for he had lost all refuge, and then he knew that had the decree fallen upon the horse, or the houses, or the like, he himself would have been saved.
Pele Yoetz 299:3: Behold, therefore, every kind of pain, loss, and suffering must be accepted with joy, and one should imagine himself as one who was sentenced to death by the government and was saved by paying some small coins, to be quit and go free. And how good and pleasant it is, for every illness and every bad dream, and for every trouble that may come, to perform the order of “redemption of the soul” arranged in the books, for charity and prayer and the power of the segulah of the Names mentioned and performed are fitting to protect and save from every trouble and distress, that there be relief.
Pele Yoetz 300:1: Peh (Mouth) — It is written (Ecclesiastes 6:7), “All the labor of man is for his mouth.” And our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Vayikra Rabbah 4:2) that all the commandments and good deeds a person performs do not suffice to atone for what he sins with his mouth. And it is written (Proverbs 21:23), “Whoever guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from troubles.” And it is written (ibid. 18:21), “Death and life are in the hand of the tongue.” And how many iniquities and sins depend on the mouth, which through our sins many have trampled upon and treated as though permitted, such as: slander, flattery, mockery, obscene speech, falsehood, vain oaths, taking the Name in vain, and many other such evils, and idle talk as bad as all of them together — one who does these things does not think he is sinning, yet they are severe transgressions, as explained in the words of our sages, of blessed memory, and we have mentioned some of them in their proper places.
Pele Yoetz 300:2: Go and learn from what was said regarding the prohibition of idle conversation, as they said in the Midrash (Shemot Rabbah 13:1): the Holy One, blessed be He, said, “The creation of the world is not laborious before Me,” as it is said (Isaiah 40:28), “He neither faints nor grows weary.” “In what am I wearied? By one who angers Me with idle words,” as it is said (Malachi 2:17), “You have wearied the Lord with your words.” And if this is so regarding idle words, how much more so when other prohibitions are mixed in with them, which is exceedingly severe, like the ropes of a cart. Over this let all who mourn mourn, and let hearts ache: how has the teaching of these prohibitions been forgotten? And not only has it been treated as permitted, but it is regarded as a mark of accomplishment to be sociable among people and to know some novel worldly matter. And how much more so if one knows how to increase laughter and the joy of frivolous company — they praise him in the gates as an entertainer, and they seek him out day after day, and his house is wide open; on the night after the conclusion of the holy Shabbat, the house fills with smoke and coffee, and flocks upon flocks gather there to pass the time until midnight. And when the novelties run out and they remain silent, they say, “What is this silence?” and they think and search for what to say — vanities of the world or forbidden speech — for “in a multitude of words transgression does not cease” (Proverbs 10:19), in order to pass the time. Woe to us from the Day of Judgment, that in a place where it is fitting to be concerned for the preciousness of time — and if we could hold back the hour with both hands so that it not pass, in order to serve our Creator with it, for one hour of Torah and good deeds in this world is better than all the life of the World to Come (Avot 4:17), and even if a man lived a thousand years, he could not fulfill his obligation and prepare provisions for his journey, and nothing exempts him, as in the statement of Rabbi Yishmael to his nephew who asked him, “As for one such as I, who has studied the entire Torah, what is the ruling regarding studying Greek wisdom?” And he answered him, “Go and find an hour that is neither day nor night [and study then]” (Menachot 99b) — and we, sinners against our own souls, seek to pass the hour and the appointed time with oaths, levity, and idle words.
Pele Yoetz 300:3: And if a man should say, “And who could do this — immediately after the conclusion of Shabbat take up a book and not increase in speech, being occupied only with Torah and necessary matters?” — hush, for this should not even be mentioned, and do not say a thing that cannot be heard, for just as it is a commandment to say a thing that will be heeded, etc. (Yevamot 65b) [i.e., one should not say things people will not accept]. For this reason I say, as the wise man said: “I will speak to a hundred; and if not, to ten; and if not, to one; and if not, to myself.” For certainly, without any doubt, this excuse does not remove a person from transgression and does not exempt him from the Day of Judgment, for this is the seduction of the evil inclination. And whatever a person desires, he can do, and according to the pain is the reward (Avot, end of ch. 5), and whoever has no regard for his Maker's honor and for his own soul is liable for his own life.
Pele Yoetz 300:4: And if a man should say, “Have we not seen upright men, and many of them, great men of Israel, who speak idle words and the like?” — you too should say to him: “Leave the great men of Israel be, for they know what they do; but we have only the words of our sages, of blessed memory, the holy ones, which are truth and whose words are truth.” And how good and pleasant it is to gather in one's free time at the house of a Torah scholar or a learned man in the city, that he read to them words of Torah, written or oral, and that they tell stories from which comes instruction in His wonders, blessed be He, and in fearing and loving the Name, and other good benefits — the words of a wise man's mouth are weighty and find favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man.
Pele Yoetz 301:1: The letter Tzadi: Tzedakah (Charity) — How great is the power of charity, who can tell? A book called “Me'il Tzedakah” was already composed by the author of Shevet Musar, and a pure man gathered all the statements of our sages, of blessed memory, in the Talmud and Midrashim, that speak of the praise of charity and how abundant its goodness is. But according to the greatness of a man's good fortune, his inclination grows stronger over him, hardening his heart so that he does not do what is fitting for him to do. And regarding such a thing they said (Eruvin 65b), “A person is recognized by his purse,” for the inclination toward the love of money is exceedingly great. Happy is one who overcomes it day by day and is saved from it — how great is his goodness, how good is his portion, and how pleasant is his lot in this world and the World to Come: wealth and riches in his house, and his righteousness endures forever, and he is a shrewd merchant who lends to the Name at a rate of a thousand for a hundred and more, and the fruit of his deeds is eaten in this world while the principal remains for the World to Come, and there is no need to elaborate on this, for well-known matters need no proof, and the whole world knows this. But this is the difficulty: that the inclination of a person's heart misleads him and shows him that his own camp is very great, and that he has already fulfilled his obligation, and that his own life comes first, and that he performs charity at all times by feeding his young and grown sons and daughters, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Ketubot 50a). But one who is righteous should examine whether he brings a tithe's worth to charity, for what he spends feeding his own sons and daughters does not count toward this, except for one whose circumstances are very pressing, as explained by the halachic authorities.
Pele Yoetz 301:2: And behold, regarding the matter of charity there are priorities, as explained in the words of our sages, of blessed memory. They said: your own life comes first, your own poor relatives come first, the poor of your city come first (Bava Metzia 71a) — in such a way that it is not fitting for a person to be excessively frugal with household expenses, without the knowledge of the household members, in order to give charity, since they come first.
Pele Yoetz 301:3: And included in the saying “your own life comes first” is that he may sell land and movable property to sustain his own dwelling, and that his soul merit to dwell honorably in the Holy Land, and that he take the foremost portion to send delights to his own soul for the World to Come; and let him not worry so much about his sons, to leave them all his wealth, for a person is closest to himself and his own life comes first. And if his offspring shall be mighty in the land, a generation of the upright shall be blessed; and if the Lord widens his boundary, then let him open his hand wide according to the blessing of the Lord that He has given him. But if his hand is short, his own life and the lives of the members of his household come before any other person, and how much more so if he has debts and does not pay them while increasing his charity — for this shall not be accepted with favor. In any case, it cannot be said that he is entirely exempt — even a poor man who is sustained by charity should give a small coin to charity every day before prayer, to fulfill what is said (Psalms 17:15), “As for me, I shall behold Your face in righteousness [charity].”
Pele Yoetz 301:4: And regarding “the poor of your city,” the commentators wrote that this refers to the poor of the Land of Israel, who are truly the poor of our city, our stronghold city. And therefore all the exiled communities have adopted the custom of giving to the emissaries of the Land of Israel — happy are the Israelites. And I say that included in “your poor” is giving to Torah scholars, for they said (Shabbat 105b) that a Torah scholar is treated by everyone as a relative. And the merit of one who supports a Torah scholar with his possessions is well known, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Kohelet Rabbah 11:1): “If you wish to give charity, give it to those who toil in Torah, as it is said, ‘Happy are you who sow beside all waters’ (Isaiah 32:20).” And how many commandments are fulfilled together thereby: charity, supporting Torah students, honoring the Torah and its students, bringing a gift to a Torah scholar, which is like offering first-fruits (Ketubot 105b), and performing charity with worthy people. And how great is his reward, as explained in the words of our sages, of blessed memory, for the deed is so great that Scripture placed Zebulun before Issachar, and the Holy One, blessed be He, is destined to provide shade and covering for the possessors of commandments alongside the possessors of Torah (Vayikra Rabbah 25:2), as it is written (Ecclesiastes 7:12), “In the shadow of wisdom, in the shadow of money,” and it is written (Psalms 119:165), “Great peace have those who love Your Torah, and nothing shall cause them to stumble.” And moreover, the needs of a Torah scholar are greater than those of other people, for he does not go about begging at doors. And he must maintain a dignified bearing, and his expenses are considerable, whether in food and drink, or in clothing and household items, since it is known that it is not their way, nor is it fitting for their honor, to be degraded in tattered rags, and they must sustain themselves with meat, wine, coffee, and the like, in order to stand guard over the Torah, for this is sound wisdom (Midrash Tehillim 7:3). And one must give them sufficient for their needs so that they not be preoccupied [with earning a living], so that their study be complete and their service whole — in such a way that happy is the man who does this and the person who holds fast to it (Isaiah 56:2); it is a tree of life to those who grasp it, and those who support it are praised (Proverbs 3:18). And there are many levels of merit in supporting Torah students and benefiting a Torah scholar from one's own possessions, as explained in the Talmud and Midrashim (Ketubot 111b). Only, one such as this cannot be expounded by a Torah scholar himself, lest it be said that he expounds for his own benefit — except that the glory of the wise is their wealth [i.e., it may be spoken of in a general, impersonal way].
Pele Yoetz 301:5: And when giving to the poor of one's city, one must distinguish which poor person is proper, modest, and worthy, and a poor person of good family who was formerly respectable — to them let him open his hand more generously, for according to what the person is, so does the value of the charity grow. But in any case, he should not refrain from giving to every one who asks and to every kind of poor person, according to the measure of his Maker, who gives bread to all flesh and whose mercies are upon all His works, and by the measure with which one measures, he is measured, for they do not scrutinize him. And what they said (Bava Batra 9a), “They stumbled them with unworthy people,” perhaps means those who do not need to take for their sustenance but take in order to spend it on a matter of transgression, may the Merciful One save us; but regarding food, they do not investigate. However, a poor man who goes about from door to door is not obligated a large gift, but is given a small gift. And it is forbidden to turn away a poor man who asks empty-handed, as it is said (Psalms 74:21), “Let not the oppressed turn back ashamed,” so ruled Maimonides (Laws of Gifts to the Poor 7:7). And it appears that this includes a poor person who extends a cloth at the entrance of the synagogue, who is like one who asks each person individually, and each person must give him a small coin.
Pele Yoetz 301:6: And likewise, the value of charity is measured according to the need, pressure, and distress of the recipient, for Maimonides ruled (ibid., 8:10) that redeeming captives takes precedence over sustaining the poor, and there is no commandment as great and important as redeeming captives. And in this manner, a person should assess the distress and pain of the poor person and have mercy on him, so that mercy be shown to him from Heaven. And accordingly, it is likewise true that timing matters, for a commandment is more valuable at its proper time, such as on the eves of festivals, and if a child is born to him, or at the marriage of his sons and daughters, when the expense and distress are great, and especially at the marriage of daughters — this is like redeeming captives, since the pressure and pain, which often lead to humiliation, are great, and the father and mother's eyes are bitter with bitter weeping, and one who has mercy shall have mercy shown to him from Heaven.
Pele Yoetz 301:7: And it would have been fitting to copy the words of Maimonides from chapter 7 of the Laws of Gifts to the Poor onward, where he speaks of the matter of charity with living, enduring, and delightful words, but I must be brief (and I still intend, with the help of Heaven, to copy his words elsewhere). But this is what he wrote there: that the highest level of charity is when the giver gives charity and does not know to whom he gives, and the recipient does not know from whom he receives, in such a way that the poor person is not shamed, and the giver performs the commandment for its own sake, not expecting to be thanked — and included in this is one who gives to the charity fund. However, it seems that if he is concerned that he will be suspected and people will wrongly say that he did not do what was fitting for him to do and that he is stingy and miserly, then, if he gives a gift to his fellow, it is a commandment to make it known to him, in order to increase love and brotherhood, peace and friendship, and because of “you shall be clear before the Lord and before Israel” (Numbers 32:22) — and this is the whole of man, that all his deeds be for the sake of Heaven.
Pele Yoetz 301:8: And included in charity given in secret is: to buy from a poor person at a higher price than he asks, and to sell to him cheaply, and to hire him for his work and pay him more than is proper for the sake of charity, and to purchase the honor of being a sandak [godfather at a circumcision] or a groomsman, for then the poor person's need is great since his expenses increase, and he is sustained with dignity, thinking that he benefits from his own labor and takes what is fitting for him, while the giver gives for the sake of charity and out of love for the commandment of sandak and groomsman, so that these commandments not be degraded, going about from door to door to be sold with no buyer, causing great disgrace. And whoever the Lord has widened his boundary should open his hand wide to do all these things according to the blessing the Lord has given him — “there is one who scatters, and yet increases” (Proverbs 11:24), that more be added to him and blessing be placed in his house, as it is written. And in truth, the inclination toward money is hard as iron, and regarding such a thing they said (Eruvin 65b), “A person is recognized by his purse” — for if in the matter of money he defeats his inclination and fulfills his obligation, he is assured that he will not sin and will fulfill every good thing. Therefore, let a man gather strength, gather great strength, to perform charity as is fitting to do, and all according to the greatness of his love for his Creator — if a man were to give all the wealth of his house for love (Song of Songs 8:7), it would be as nothing before it — and how much more so knowing and believing in our holy Torah and the words of our sages, of blessed memory, that the Name shall repay manifold, and a person is never impoverished by charity (Maimonides, Laws of Gifts to the Poor 10:2), and no evil thing or harm ever comes about because of charity, as it is said (Isaiah 32:17), “And the work of righteousness shall be peace.”
Pele Yoetz 302:1: Tze'akah (Outcry) — How great is the power of an outcry to annul a decree, as it is written (Psalms 34:17-18), “The face of the Lord is against evildoers, to cut off their remembrance from the earth” — [yet] “they cried out, and the Lord heard.” And likewise regarding the four who must give thanks, it is written (Psalms 107:6), “Then they cried out to the Lord in their trouble, and He saved them from their distresses.” And behold, the plain meaning of the word “tze'akah” [outcry] is the remnant of a voice in prayer from within the walls of one's heart. Yet the heart hesitates regarding this, for they said (Berachot 24b), “One who raises his voice in his prayer is among the false prophets.” And according to what is derived from the camp [of Israel], as it is written (I Samuel 1:13) [of Hannah], “And her voice was not heard,” it implies that even in a personal prayer that one prays over his own trouble, he must not let his voice be heard. And the holy Zohar was even stricter, saying (part 1, p. 209) that one who lets his voice be heard in his prayer, his prayer is not heard on high. But there are other places in the holy Zohar that imply that it is fitting to raise a soft voice while praying. And it seems fitting to somewhat reconcile the matter's meaning: that it is best that his heart cry out a great and bitter cry, while the voice remains low, only his lips moving, his voice not heard. Yet if a fire burns within him and he cannot restrain himself from crying out in a loud voice from within his trouble, this too is exceedingly worthy and bears fruit above. And how much more so if he is the prayer leader who passes before the ark, who is compelled to cry out in a great voice. And the essence of the outcry depends on the heart, with the voice at a medium level, the voice of weeping, as one who cries and weeps and entreats — and by this God shall hear and answer them, for He hears the outcry of His people in public.
Pele Yoetz 303:1: Tzavaah (Testament) — It is good for a man to command his sons and his household after him, that they keep the way of the Lord, for it is the nature of man that he more readily heeds and fulfills the command of his father and mother than he heeds and observes and fulfills the Ten Commandments; and it turns out that his name shall be remembered for good, and the great merit of his sons' merit depends on him. But he must know his sons according to what they are, and not burden them with something he fears they will not fulfill and thereby add transgression and sin, causing them to be punished on his account, for we find that Heaven is more strict and punishes more for transgressing a father's command than for transgressing the words of the Torah. Let him rather do this: let him write in his own handwriting, “This is the evil way and this is the straight way,” not in the manner of a command and warning, but merely as a reminder, and whoever heeds it, blessing shall come upon him.
Pele Yoetz 303:2: And it is likewise good for a man to command regarding himself that all that is in their power be done for his repose and the elevation of his soul. Let him give instructions regarding the matter of washing, burial, a tombstone, distribution of charity, study sessions, and prayers for his repose, for who is concerned for his own soul more than he himself? And even if he trusts his sons to do much for him, he should not refrain from commanding it and writing it down, so that it be a reminder before their eyes to give it preference. And how much more so since, through our sins, there are sons who are unreliable, who forget their father and mother from their heart, do not remember or take note or bring them to mind, except a very little on the yahrzeit day. Woe to such sons, and woe to such fathers who look to their sons' table — and it is best for a man's charity to precede him [in his lifetime]. And let him also command his sons to act on his behalf and send delicacies to his soul as he loved.
Pele Yoetz 303:3: And it is likewise good for a man to arrange his affairs and write down clearly whom he owes and who owes him, and to decree with all firmness that they fulfill everything found written in his ledger, and pay in full every creditor, without any claim or dispute, so that his soul may rest. And let him divide his property among his sons in a proper order, so that there be no jealousy among them, and so that no dispute or quarrel remain among them after him. And let him command them that there be love and brotherhood, peace and friendship among them, and that each help his brother. Such and such things let him command his sons and his household according to what they are, and according to the need of the hour let the wise man hear and add learning.
Pele Yoetz 303:4: And behold, following the way they said (Shabbat 153a), “Repent one day before your death,” meaning let him repent today lest he die tomorrow — so it is with this matter, that he should not delay making his will until the end comes, for a person does not know his time, and he must be concerned lest, God forbid, his misfortune come suddenly, and lest he die in his youth a sudden death, God forbid; and even if he becomes ill, he might fall into a stupor in his illness and be unable to do anything; and furthermore, at that time the man himself would tremble and also be concerned about the alarm of the household members, and at that point his mind is confused and cannot settle upon it. Therefore this is the straight way: that while he is still in his youth and health, his will should be written, and he should command with all firmness that what is found written be fulfilled after his death. And day by day let him add, subtract, and change as he wishes, according to what he sees fit. And when he divides his property, if he sees that the Lord has widened his boundary, let him not leave all his wealth to others, but rather take for himself the foremost portion, that it be a permanent fund in trustworthy hands, and let the returns be sent to him as delights for his soul — this is the straight way, glorious to those who do it and glorious to him among men (Avot 2:1; Nedarim 22b).
Pele Yoetz 303:5: And it is fitting for every person to be concerned to fulfill the testaments of Rabbi Yehudah HeChasid, for these are ancient matters, and whoever knows them and transgresses his words is liable for his own soul, while one who heeds him guards his own soul.
Pele Yoetz 304:1: Tzeniut (Modesty) — This trait is needed by men, and how much more so by women, and through it a person is distinguished from an animal. And the trait of modesty is required even when one is alone in the innermost chambers, because of the honor of the King, exalted and lofty, awesome and fearsome, whose glory fills the whole earth — for our master ruled in the Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chaim, sec. 2, para. 1) that one should not put on his undergarment while standing, but rather while still lying down, insert his head and arms in such a way that when he rises his body is found covered. And from this we may infer regarding Friday evening, when he changes his undergarment, that he must do so in a manner that his body not be exposed. And likewise our master ruled (ibid., sec. 3, para. 4) that one must be modest in the privy, and not expose himself except a handbreadth behind him and a handbreadth in front of him. And a woman must be especially modest in the privy, and should not enter the privy [in front of others], nor recite the blessing “Asher Yatzar” [Who Formed] in the presence of men.
Pele Yoetz 304:2: And the essence of modesty is required in the matter of marital relations, that the woman be careful and guard that no one sense or know when she goes to immerse for her husband. And at the time of relations, he should be exceedingly, exceedingly modest, so that no created being sense it, not even a small child. And likewise the woman should be modest — “all the glory of the king's daughter is within” — and she should not converse excessively even with her relatives, and even with her husband, for it is written (Amos 4:13), “And tells man what is his speech,” and our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Chagigah 5b) that even for a light conversation between a man and his wife, he is destined to give an account.
Pele Yoetz 304:3: And likewise the trait of modesty is needed regarding Torah and commandments, as it is written (Micah 6:8), “And to walk humbly with your God.” And it is written (Proverbs 11:2), “And with the modest is wisdom.”
Pele Yoetz 305:1: Tzitzit — The commandment of tzitzit is equal to all the commandments (Nedarim 25a), and this is an opening to the completion of the 248 limbs and 365 sinews of one's soul, spirit, and higher soul, since we are unable to fulfill the 613 commandments — when we fulfill the commandment of tzitzit, it is considered as though we had fulfilled the 613 commandments. But one must have this specific intention explicitly, and it is good to say so before putting on the tzitzit:
Pele Yoetz 305:2: “May it be Your will, O Lord our God and God of our fathers, that You accept with mercy and favor this commandment of tzitzit that we perform, as though we had fulfilled it in all its particulars, its refinements, and its precise details, and as though we had fulfilled all 613 commandments that depend upon it.”
Pele Yoetz 305:3: And therefore one must be careful never to be without a small tallit [tzitzit garment] upon him, and he must be careful, whether with a large tallit or a small tallit, that it be valid according to its law and all its rules; for if he is not careful, it turns out that he has not fulfilled the commandment, and its absence would have been better, since by putting on a four-cornered garment with invalid tzitzit, he commits a transgression, reciting a blessing in vain and wearing a four-cornered garment without [proper] tzitzit. And he must likewise be careful to fulfill in this the verse “This is my God and I will glorify Him” (Exodus 15:2) with a beautiful tallit, for if he wears fine garments, various fine articles, while the tallit over his garments is torn and worn out, will he not be ashamed in this world and disgraced in the World to Come, and cause disgrace and wrath?
Pele Yoetz 305:4: And he should be careful to make the tallit, whether small or large, from sheep's wool and not from other materials, for then he fulfills only a rabbinic commandment (Orach Chaim, sec. 9, para. 1), and this is like one who could earn a thousand gold coins but settles for five hundred.
Pele Yoetz 305:5: And it is fitting to educate children in this commandment, that they have a small tallit under their garments constantly, and thereby they shall acquire an order of holiness and have assistance in Torah and Divine service. And the holy Zohar elaborated greatly (Parashat Vaetchanan, p. 265) on the praise that comes to one who leaves his house wrapped in tzitzit and crowned with tefillin — happy is he who can do this.
Pele Yoetz 306:1: Tza'ar (Pain/Grief) — It is not fitting to grieve over anything in the world except grief over Heaven, for over the vanities of the world there is no room to grieve, since all is vanity. And it has already been said that the Holy One, blessed be He, does not spare the righteous from suffering, that they are made to suffer, or that they themselves grieve over the events of the time — for this is comparable to a father who watches his son when he is a small child building a house out of little sticks and straw, rejoicing in it, and a man comes and destroys his structure, and the child goes to his father and complains about him, crying bitterly, thinking that his father should have killed that man; but his father laughs and is not concerned at all, for he truly knows that his son's grief is vanity and emptiness, only that according to the child's own understanding and limited comprehension he grieves greatly — so it is with this matter. The grief that a person feels over the affairs of this world is all vanity and vexation of spirit. And just as sometimes the father helps the son build these houses, and buys him things that are children's playthings, in order to give him satisfaction according to his own understanding, so the Holy One, blessed be He, sometimes fulfills a person's desire in the affairs of this world according to his own understanding, since his soul desires them, in order to give him satisfaction. And if the Holy One, blessed be He, causes a person pain through various forms of suffering to atone for his sins, and he grieves and weeps, the Holy One, blessed be He, is not concerned about him, even though He is merciful and gracious, the Master of mercy — for this is comparable to an infant whose mother washes off his filth and he cries and weeps, yet his mother is not concerned about him. And like a doctor who administers harsh remedies to a patient, and sometimes amputates a limb, and is not concerned about his pain, for he knows it is for his benefit and good — so it is with this matter, for whatever the Merciful One does, He does for the good. And the man who understands this should not grieve at all.
Pele Yoetz 306:2: And in the book Shnei Luchot HaBrit there is a story about a pious man who entered a city and saw the people sad and bitter, while he himself was joyful and glad-hearted, dancing and leaping. And the people of the city said to him, “Why do you rejoice thus?” He said to them, “Why should I not rejoice?” They said to him, “Do you not see all the people weeping, each at the entrance of his tent, and why do you laugh among the weeping?” He said to them, “Let me give you a parable: to one who entered a house and found them sleeping and dreaming frightening dreams, weeping in their sleep — would one who sees this grieve? Does he not know that this is only a dream, and once he wakes from his sleep he shall find rest?” So it is with this matter: all who grieve over the affairs of this world are like dreamers, and I, who am awake, know that all is vanity. But over grief concerning Heaven, it is an obligation to grieve, and from this follows every kind of grief that one must feel over sins, iniquities, and transgressions — not for himself, that he shall suffer harsh punishments, but because he causes grief and anger to the King of glory.
Pele Yoetz 306:3: And likewise it is fitting to grieve over the destruction of the Holy Temple, destroyed through our sins — not because we are exiled, afflicted, and downtrodden, but because of the grief of Heaven, which is exceedingly great; and so regarding every kind of suffering, this shall be his grief: that it caused anger and pain to the King, exalted and lofty, as it is written (Isaiah 63:9), “In all their affliction He was afflicted.” And this is comparable to a son who loves his father, and angered him so greatly that the father was forced to set aside his mercy and strike him a severe blow — for if the son is a faithful lover, he is not at all concerned about his own wounds, but only about his father's anger and grief, thinking, “What shall I do, and how shall I appease my father, so that he have no more grief and anger because of me?” And how much more so knowing that the mercies of Heaven are abundant, and His attribute is to do good beyond measure, and His love for His people Israel is great, and the measure of His grief corresponds to His foundations, as it is written (Exodus 19:21), “lest many of them fall,” and our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Mechilta, Parashat Yitro, ch. 4) that even one who falls is considered great in His eyes. If so, it is fitting to grieve over the sufferings, on the one hand, because it was certainly a great anger to our Father in Heaven, to the point that He was forced to strike him such a severe blow. And at the time a person grieves, the Divine Presence grieves — what does the tongue say? “My head is heavy for Me, My arm is heavy for Me,” etc.
Pele Yoetz 306:4: And this is the reason one must grieve with anguish of soul over the loss of the righteous, and over all the sufferings of the righteous, who are profaned because of our transgressions and crushed because of our iniquities, and because of the evil the righteous man is gathered in [dies], and the grief of Heaven grows great because men of faith have perished, who came by the power of their deeds, etc. And even for righteous men who died in earlier years one must grieve, as they said (Zohar part 3, p. 57) that whoever grieves on Yom Kippur over the death of Aaron's sons is forgiven all his sins. And the reason is that the living should take to heart: if the flame fell upon the cedars, what shall the hyssops of the wall do? And let him further take to heart that, through our many sins, faithful men have ceased among mankind, and the pious have perished from the earth, and there is no upright man among men, and the Holy One, blessed be He, has no one in His world with whom to delight in love as in days of old and years of ancient times, and this is because of our sins, as they said in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 11a): “Such-and-such a rabbi deserved that the Divine Presence rest upon him, but his generation was not worthy of it.” And because the generations diminish, Torah likewise goes and diminishes, going and decreasing. Over this it is fitting to feel bitter and grieve with a stirring grief.
Pele Yoetz 306:5: And the kabbalists wrote that the sins of the wicked and the strengthening of the husks [kelipot] because of them cause confusion in the thoughts of the righteous, so that they cannot serve their Creator with a complete service and cling to Him as is fitting. For this let our hearts tremble and leap from their place, and let us weep bitterly over such a great evil, and over the many such evils and troubles we have caused above through our sins.
Pele Yoetz 306:6: And behold, if a person grieves over the vanities of this world, this is a lack of understanding, as we wrote above in the name of the author of Sefer HaBrit: for whichever way you look at it, if it is a matter that has a remedy, let him make the remedy and be saved; and if it has no remedy, what does his grief give him, add to him, or benefit him? But one who grieves over grief concerning Heaven — his grief makes an impression and bears fruit. It makes an impression in that it is proper conduct and part of complete character traits that a person's disposition be sociable with others, and that he grieve, or at least show grief and weep with those who weep. And how much disgrace comes to those who go to a burial, and while they are preparing the grave, the relatives of the deceased sit near the deceased, bitter of soul, and they [the others] increase in drinking and laughter and levity, at that very time, in that very place, in front of the deceased and his relatives — this is certainly a very shameful, evil, and bitter thing, and it is fitting to protest against it if they will listen, that this evil custom be uprooted and there be no such thing in Israel.
Pele Yoetz 306:7: And how much more so if his father, mother, and relatives are in grief, in which he is obligated to grieve with them, and this is half a comfort to a person, that he sees others grieving with him in his trouble. So too, in this manner, a person who grieves over grief concerning Heaven, according to his grief, gives satisfaction to his Maker, and according to the pain is the reward. And it bears fruit in that, according to his grief, he shall increase his effort to rectify what he has distorted and to do all that is in his power to do, in order to ease the grief of his Father in Heaven, like a son who loves his father and sees him in a stirring grief on his account, whose flesh pains him and who gives his life to save him from his trouble. And the kabbalists have already written that according to the sorrow, sighing, and grief with which a person grieves over his sins, so shall he increase in purifying the purity of his soul. Behold, therefore, how precious are the words of the wise man (Mivchar HaPeninim 44, 46), who said to one whom he saw in grief: “If your grief is over the affairs of this world, the Holy One, blessed be He, shall remove your grief from you; but if your grief is over grief concerning Heaven, the Holy One, blessed be He, shall add to you grief upon grief.”
Pele Yoetz 306:8: And behold, the matter of grief is something entrusted to the heart, and the nearby inclination substitutes its counterfeit and introduces grief over the vanities of this world, while grief concerning Heaven is forgotten from the heart, neither felt nor sensed. And the man who is pure shall strengthen himself with pure thoughts to do each thing in its proper time, according to its measure, not exchanging or substituting it, for one who comes to purify himself is assisted [from Heaven] (Shabbat 104a). And it is known what is written in the book of Ben Sira (cited in Yevamot 63b), “Do not grieve over tomorrow's trouble,” etc. And since His right hand's shadow is over the earth, what advantage does a person have in all his toil if he lives a life of grief? There is nothing good for a person except that he rejoice in his portion, trust in the Name, and do good.
Pele Yoetz 307:1: Tzarah (Trouble) — Over every trouble that comes upon a person, it is fitting to take it to heart and search his deeds, for God has made it so that people fear before Him, and He sends some trouble upon a person so that he take it to heart to repent — an atonement He prepares in order to direct it to its furrows. And if on a day of trouble he does not take it to heart to repent, but attributes the matter to chance, behold, his punishment is explicit in the Torah, in Parashat Bechukotai, as it is written (Leviticus 26), “And if by these you will not be disciplined by Me, but walk with Me in happenstance, then I too will walk with you in happenstance, and I will continue to strike you,” etc. Therefore let him not fail, at the time of trouble, to accept upon himself to repent from whatever transgressions are in his hand, and through this the Almighty shall be entreated for him and heal him.
Pele Yoetz 307:2: And there are further three good things for every trouble, to annul the decree, and they are: fast, voice, money. Fast: let him afflict his soul with a fast, for a fast stands in place of a sacrifice and is accepted as atonement for him. And Israel has already been accustomed from ancient days, for every trouble, to decree a fast upon the community, as we have learned in Tractate Ta'anit. Go and learn how great is the power of a fast to annul a decree, to the point that even on a Shabbat when the Ninth of Av is postponed because of it, they permitted fasting a “dream fast” (Shabbat 11a), since it has become an accepted matter among the holy sages that it is effective to annul a decree; but the fast must be of the kind the blessed God would choose, as will be written further under the entry “Ta'anit,” with the help of Heaven. And Voice: the voice, the voice of Jacob, is what helps them at the time of their trouble. And there are two kinds of voices: the voice of Torah and the voice of prayer and supplication. Torah: let him engage in Torah. And it is written in the books that reciting the Book of Psalms with intention and humility, and especially with ten men, is very effective for warding off any trouble and for saving from every trouble. And likewise there is a segulah found in the books: for any trouble that may befall a city, to read all the verses of Psalms that begin with the letters of the city's name. And let him pour out his soul in prayer before the Name, who answers His people Israel at a time of trouble. And how good it is if there is a Torah scholar who knows how to arrange a fitting prayer according to the trouble. And thoughts of repentance must precede prayer, and one must mention at the beginning of the supplication matters of confession, remorse, and humility, so that the prayer be favorable and accepted, as I shall write further under the entry “Tefillah” [Prayer]. Our sages, of blessed memory, said further (Sanhedrin 44b), “A person should always precede trouble with prayer, for had Abraham not preceded to pray between Bethel and Ai, no remnant or survivor would have been left of the enemies of Israel.” We thus learn that even for one's offspring far into the future one must precede to pray. (And if God be with me, without a vow, I shall arrange, with the help of Heaven, a personal prayer to be recited for every kind of trouble and the evils that arise to come upon the world, that a person recite it at least at a favorable time during the Ten Days of Repentance, and I have set it in place in my House of Prayers, with the help of Heaven.)
